title: You Should Use Mini Whiteboards
author: Dylan Kane
summary: Dylan Kane makes the case that mini whiteboards are the single teaching tool he would recommend above all others, because they let a teacher sample the whole class's understanding in seconds and adjust instruction minute-to-minute. He's careful to frame them as a supplement, not a replacement, for pencil-and-paper work: a typical class might use two rounds of 1-5 questions on whiteboards, reserved for moments where a quick, whole-class check matters more than volume of practice. The bulk of the piece catalogues concrete use cases — prerequisite knowledge checks, checking retention of yesterday's lesson, readiness checks before independent practice, checking 'atoms' of a broken-down skill, stamping learning after a class discussion, and stepping through multi-step problems one step at a time. A long Q&A section addresses the practical mechanics that make or break the system in real classrooms: preventing copying with 'flip and hover,' handling students who leave boards blank (distinguishing confusion from opting out), managing unkind reactions to wrong answers, storage and marker logistics, and the multi-year process of refining the routine. Kane credits Adam Boxer's writing and webinars as a major influence and is candid that adopting mini whiteboards did not transform his classroom overnight — it surfaced discouraging results before it drove the gradual instructional changes that ultimately helped.
points: Kane's core practical claim: mini whiteboards should be a small, targeted supplement (roughly two rounds of 1-5 questions per class) used for whole-class checks, not the primary vehicle for student practice, which stays pencil-and-paper.
His 'flip and hover' routine (write the answer, flip the board upside down, hold it hovering above the desk) solves two problems at once — reducing copying and signalling who's finished.
He explicitly separates two distinct benefits: an in-the-moment check for understanding, versus a longer-run 'barometer' that reveals whether broader changes to his teaching are actually working.
His advice on non-participation is diagnostic, not punitive: distinguish students who are confused (who need support) from students who are opting out (who need nudges, then individual follow-up).

Kane is candid that the tool didn't transform his classroom overnight — early use surfaced discouraging results (half the class wrong) before it drove the slower instructional changes that actually improved outcomes.
quotes: This is the absolute best way to check for understanding. In very little time, I can sample the entire class and get a sense of what students know and don't know. The activity is flexible: I can ask as many or as few questions as I want, I can adjust in response to student answers, and we can do a quick reteach and practice on the whiteboards if necessary.

Mini whiteboards are a bit slow: I ask a question, then I wait until every student has a chance to answer, then students hold their boards up, then I take a moment to scan, and then we are on to the next question.

So here's the routine: students write their answer to a question, then they 'flip and hover': they flip the whiteboard upside down and hold it hovering above the desk. This serves two purposes: one, it reduces cheating, and two, it signals for you which students are finished.
In all of this I have to distinguish between students who are confused, and students who are opting out. If a student is confused, I offer them support and make sure it isn't framed as a punishment.
This felt really hard. And in the long term, this type of checking for understanding drove a ton of positive changes in my teaching.

The second benefit is that mini whiteboards give broader insight into whether my teaching is working. If, over and over again, students don't remember what they were supposed to have learned, then something is wrong.
